steps.step: Discovery working session with champion and 2-3 engineering leads
steps.exit: Named systems, pains and the people who feel them, written down

steps.step: Agree the one metric that matters and capture its baseline
steps.exit: Baseline number, data source and owner

steps.step: Identify the economic buyer and confirm their priorities
steps.exit: EB named; meeting scheduled or held

steps.step: Draft pilot scope: repositories, teams, use cases
steps.exit: Scope document reviewed by champion

steps.step: Submit to AI governance and cyber risk review
steps.exit: Review date booked; questionnaire received

steps.step: Start supplier onboarding and security questionnaires
steps.exit: Vendor record opened; questionnaires returned

steps.step: Architecture review: identity, repo access, network, data handling
steps.exit: Approved access pattern for the pilot

steps.step: Sign pilot success criteria tied to the baseline metric
steps.exit: Signed success criteria with thresholds

steps.step: Audit: Code Scan on one legacy repository
steps.exit: Findings reviewed; first pull requests merged

steps.step: Review: REVIEW.md plus Devin Review and Autofix on live pull requests
steps.exit: Review time and merge rate measured against baseline

steps.step: Modernize: one bounded migration as a Dynamic Workflow
steps.exit: Migration plan versioned; changes merged and tested

steps.step: Operate: Devin Oncall on one service, human approves fixes
steps.exit: Time to root cause measured on real alerts

steps.step: Weekly readout to champion; fortnightly to EB staff
steps.exit: Readouts delivered on schedule

steps.step: Build the business case against the baseline and SI or contractor spend
steps.exit: Business case reviewed by champion and finance partner

steps.step: Competitive and do-nothing comparison documented
steps.exit: Customer has stated why Devin over alternatives

steps.step: Economic buyer readout and decision
steps.exit: Verbal decision and budget source confirmed

steps.step: MSA, data processing and AI addendum redlines
steps.exit: Legal redlines closed

steps.step: Procurement approval and purchase order
steps.exit: PO issued

steps.step: Signature by authorized signatory
steps.exit: Signed agreement

steps.step: Enablement for first teams; REVIEW.md and playbooks per team
steps.exit: Teams active; usage and cost visible per team

steps.step: Expansion plan to the next business unit or program
steps.exit: Next scope and sponsor agreed

trees.title: M · Metrics
trees.open: If this works, what number changes, and who in leadership watches that number?

branches.if: Names a business number (backlog, MTTR, SI spend)
branches.say: What is it today, where does that figure come from, and what would a good year look like?

then.say: Let's write that into the pilot success criteria with a threshold we both agree on.
then.next: Signed success criteria on the MAP. M confirmed.

then.say: Who could pull it in the next two weeks? We can't prove value without a starting point.
then.next: Baseline owner and date on the MAP. M partly confirmed.

branches.say: How would your CFO see that show up: fewer contractor hours, programs delivered sooner, or fewer incidents?

then.say: Which program or team would show it first?
then.next: Tie the metric to a named program. M hypothesis.

then.say: Teams like yours often use cost per merged change or time to retire a legacy component. Would either matter here?
then.next: Offer two metrics to choose from. M still unknown.

branches.say: How do leaders decide today whether an engineering investment paid off?

then.say: Then a pilot with one clear number would be new for them. What would they find most convincing?
then.next: Co-design the metric with the champion. M hypothesis.

trees.title: E · Economic buyer
trees.open: Who would have to say yes to spend money on this, and whose budget would it come from?

branches.say: What does that person care about most this year, and how have they made similar decisions before?

then.say: Can you set up 30 minutes with them after our first pilot readout? I'll bring the numbers.
then.next: EB meeting on the MAP. E partly confirmed.

then.say: Who on their staff would know? Could we meet them first?
then.next: Find a path to the EB through staff. E hypothesis.

branches.say: Who on that committee carries the most weight, and who can stop a decision alone?

then.say: How do we get time with them before the committee meets?
then.next: EB identified within the committee. E partly confirmed.

then.say: Who sets the committee's agenda and budget?
then.next: Find who owns the budget line. E still unknown.

branches.say: Where does application maintenance and SI spend sit today, and who owns it?

then.say: If we show we can move some of that work faster, would they want to see it?
then.next: Reframe budget as redeployed spend. E hypothesis.

trees.title: D · Decision criteria
trees.open: When you look at an AI agent for real engineering work, what will it have to prove?

branches.say: Can we get those requirements in writing so our security team can answer each one?

then.say: Thank you. Can we also add that every change must arrive tested and recorded? That protects your reviewers.
then.next: Criteria include proof-of-work. D partly confirmed.

then.say: Would it help if we drafted a starting list from what other energy teams ask, for you to edit?
then.next: Draft criteria together. D hypothesis.

branches.say: Which operating systems, repositories and tools does it have to work with?

then.say: Devin works in its own Windows, Linux and macOS machines and in Microsoft Teams. Can we make 'works on our real platforms' a criterion?
then.next: Platform criterion favors Devin. D partly confirmed.

branches.say: How will you compare cost: per seat, per task, or against the work it replaces?

then.say: Agents do whole tasks, so cost per merged change is a fairer comparison. Would finance accept that?
then.next: Shift to outcome-based cost. D hypothesis.

trees.title: D · Decision process
trees.open: Walk me through what happens between a pilot that works and a signed agreement.

branches.say: Who owns each step, and how long did each take last time?

then.say: Let's put those on a shared plan with dates and work back from your budget date.
then.next: MAP populated with owners. D confirmed.

branches.say: How did the last developer tool or platform get approved here?

then.say: Who was involved, and what nearly stopped it?
then.next: Map the real process from precedent. D partly confirmed.

then.say: Who would know? Could we ask procurement or the architecture board together?
then.next: Joint discovery with procurement. D hypothesis.

trees.title: P · Paper process
trees.open: Once the business says yes, what has to happen for a contract to get signed?

branches.say: Can we start supplier onboarding and the security questionnaire now, during the pilot?

then.say: Who should I send the onboarding packet to today?
then.next: Onboarding started. P partly confirmed.

then.say: What is the usual time from selection to signature? Let's plan the pilot end date around it.
then.next: Close date reflects paper time. P hypothesis.

branches.say: Is there a standard AI addendum, and who in legal owns it?

then.say: Could we share our terms with them early so redlines run in parallel?
then.next: Legal engaged early. P partly confirmed.

trees.title: I · Identify pain
trees.open: What is the engineering problem that is costing you the most right now?

branches.say: What has it cost so far, and who feels it most?

then.say: What happens if it is still a problem a year from now?
then.next: Pain tied to cost, person and consequence. I confirmed.

then.say: Who could put a number on it? It matters for making the case to leadership.
then.next: Find the cost owner. I partly confirmed.

branches.say: Where is your team spending time it would rather spend elsewhere?

then.say: Which piece of that toil is the most repetitive and the most painful?
then.next: Narrow to a concrete pain. I hypothesis.

then.say: What is leadership asking for that the team cannot deliver yet?
then.next: Look for future pain. I still unknown.

trees.title: C · Champion
trees.open: If this goes well, what does it mean for you and your team?

branches.say: Who else needs to believe in this for it to happen, and can you get me in front of them?

then.say: What should I know about each of them before we meet?
then.next: Champion shares access and insight. C confirmed.

then.say: What would make you comfortable introducing us? Is there something you need from me first?
then.next: Test whether they are a coach or a champion. C partly confirmed.

branches.say: Who in your organization would be most affected by solving this?

then.say: Would you introduce us? It sounds like they own this problem.
then.next: Find the real champion. C hypothesis.

trees.title: C · Competition
trees.open: What else are you looking at, including building it yourselves or leaving things as they are?

branches.say: What do you want it to do that it doesn't do today?

then.say: That's the work Devin does end to end. Could we compare on one of those jobs?
then.next: Side-by-side on Devin's strengths. C partly confirmed.

branches.say: What would your team rather spend its time on than maintaining agent infrastructure?

then.say: Then Devin can carry the engineering backlog while your team builds what's unique to you.
then.next: Turn the build team into allies. C partly confirmed.

branches.say: How is that work measured today, and what would you change?

then.say: Would it help to show what the same work looks like with agents doing the heavy lifting?
then.next: SI spend in the business case. C partly confirmed.

branches.say: What does waiting a year cost, in backlog, risk or spend?

then.say: Let's put that cost next to the pilot cost for your leadership.
then.next: Status quo priced. C partly confirmed.

trees.title: Executive: revenue, profitability and risk
trees.open: You've committed publicly to a savings and margin number. Which technology programs does that depend on most?

branches.say: If that program slipped two quarters, what would it do to the year?

then.say: Who owns that program day to day? I'd like to show them how we take engineering work off the critical path, with weekly evidence you can see.
then.next: Introduction to the program owner; EB identified (E, I).

then.say: What gives you that confidence, and what would change it?
then.next: Probe execution risk with the program owner (I).

branches.say: Where does the run-and-maintain spend on your application portfolio sit in the cost targets?

then.say: Then moving that work from people-hours to agent-hours is a savings line. Who would own that analysis?
then.next: Finance partner or CIO for a business case (M, E).

then.say: What risk is the board asking about most this year?
then.next: Find the risk angle: cyber, execution or key people (I).

branches.say: Most companies can't tie AI spend to output yet. We show cost per task and the work it produced. Which part of the business would you want to see that in first?

then.say: Who leads technology for that business?
then.next: Referral down to L3 with executive air cover (E, C).

trees.title: Cold open to a CIO on cost
trees.open: AI spend is turning into its own line item while modernization budgets stay flat. How are you deciding what AI work is worth paying for?

branches.if: "We have a governance group handling that."
branches.say: What has that group approved so far, and what have they measured afterwards?

then.say: Which of those would you want a software agent to move? We can baseline it in a pilot.
then.next: Agree the metric and a discovery session (M, I).

then.say: Most teams we talk to are in the same place. Teams moving fastest measure cost per merged change and time to retire legacy components. Would those work here?
then.next: Offer a metric workshop with their team (M).

branches.say: Where has it helped, and which large jobs, like migrations or audits, still haven't moved?

then.say: What has that delay cost, and who is accountable for it?
then.next: Move to the modernization tree; find the owner (I, E).

then.say: How much of your budget goes to run-and-maintain, and is that where you want it in three years?
then.next: Probe SI and maintenance spend (M, C).

branches.say: Understood. What is the priority this year, and where is engineering capacity the constraint on it?

then.say: That is the problem Devin is built for. Who runs that program?
then.next: Ask for an introduction to the program owner (C).

then.say: Then I'd suggest we stay in touch. Can I send you a short brief on what changed this quarter?
then.next: Send the customer brief; nurture.

trees.title: Modernization lead
trees.open: If you could retire one system this year at a tenth of the usual cost, which would it be?

branches.say: What makes it hard: the code, the testing, the people who know it, or the integrations?

then.say: We would start with a Code Scan to inventory and classify it, then split the work across parallel Devins with a plan you can read and version. Every change comes back tested and recorded.
then.next: Propose an audit on that repository (I, D).

then.say: How is that knowledge captured today? Devin builds memory of how each team works, in readable files you can govern.
then.next: Pair memory with the audit (I, D).

then.say: Which systems does it touch, and where do they run? Devin works in its own Windows, Linux and macOS machines.
then.next: Architecture session with platform lead (D).

branches.say: How do you prioritize them today, and who signs off on that list?

then.say: Which item on that list has the clearest cost of delay?
then.next: Pick a pilot target and its baseline (M).

then.say: A Code Scan across a few candidates can rank them by effort and risk. Would that help you make the call?
then.next: Offer a multi-repo scan (I).

branches.say: How is that contract measured, and how do you feel about the pace?

then.say: What would it mean if your own team could move faster with agents doing the heavy lifting?
then.next: Bring SI spend into the business case (M, C).

then.say: Could the SI use Devin too? Some teams want their partners working faster on the same contract.
then.next: Explore a partner-led motion (C).

trees.title: "We already have Copilot"
trees.open: That's common. What do your teams use it for day to day?

branches.say: How has it changed the big jobs, such as migrations, upgrades, audits and on-call?

then.say: Devin is built for those. It works end to end in its own machine and hands back tested, recorded changes. The two can live side by side.
then.next: Position as complementary; pick a large job (D, C).

then.say: Where did it stop short, and what would finishing that work be worth?
then.next: Quantify the gap (M).

branches.say: What are you measuring in that pilot, and how is it going against those measures?

then.say: What would you need to see to call an agent pilot a success? We'd be glad to run against the same criteria.
then.next: Shape side-by-side criteria (D).

then.say: Which work is out of its reach today, such as Windows builds, codebase-wide scans or on-call?
then.next: Find the gap Devin fills (D, C).

branches.say: Makes sense. Devin works natively in Microsoft Teams and Microsoft 365, so it fits the same environment. What work would you want an agent to own?

then.say: Let's scope that as a pilot with a clear baseline.
then.next: Move to the MAP (M, D).

then.say: Where does application maintenance and SI spend sit? That is often where agent budgets come from.
then.next: Find the EB and the budget line (E).

trees.title: "We build our own"
trees.open: Your team clearly knows this space. What have you built so far, and what's next on the roadmap?

branches.say: Where is your team's time going: building the platform, or building the products the business is asking for?

then.say: Devin can carry the engineering backlog so your team focuses on what is unique to you. The agent's machines, verification and memory are already built.
then.next: Position as capacity, not replacement (C).

then.say: Which parts would you rather not maintain yourselves, like isolated machines across operating systems, or on-call tooling?
then.next: Find buy-versus-build seams (D).

branches.say: What have you learned about reliability on long tasks?

then.say: That matches what builders reported all quarter: verification is where the work is. Devin tests and records each change. Want to compare on one of your tasks?
then.next: Offer a bake-off on their task (D).

then.say: How will you handle cost and model choice as models change every month?
then.next: Introduce Fusion and per-session cost (D, M).

trees.title: Security and data concerns
trees.open: Before anything else, what would you need to know about how an agent handles your code and data?

branches.say: Let's get your requirements in writing and have our security team respond in detail. Who should be in that session?

then.say: I'll set up the session and bring the documentation to it.
then.next: Security review on the MAP (D, P). Confirm Cognition's terms internally first.

then.say: Happy to. Can we start it now, in parallel with discovery, so it doesn't hold up a pilot?
then.next: Start the paper process early (P).

branches.say: What controls do you apply to service accounts and contractors today?

then.say: We'd mirror those for Devin: scoped access, its own isolated machine, and every change reviewed by a person.
then.next: Architecture review (D).

then.say: Would it help to start with a read-only Code Scan, where Devin proposes changes but merges nothing?
then.next: Low-risk first step (D).

branches.say: How long does a critical finding stay open today, and what slows it down?

then.say: Security Swarm finds exploitable issues, proves them in a sandbox and opens the fix as a pull request. Want to try it on one application?
then.next: Security pilot (I, M).

then.say: What about code your team doesn't own, like acquired or vendor-modified applications?
then.next: Find the uncovered estate (I).

trees.title: Operations and on-call
trees.open: Who takes the first look at an alert at night, and how long until you know the root cause?

branches.if: Senior engineers, it takes a while
branches.say: What does that do to their week, and to the roadmap?

then.say: Devin Oncall takes the first pass, investigates, and comes back with a root cause and a tested fix for a person to approve. AngelList put Devin on its on-call rotation.
then.next: Pilot on one service (I, M).

then.say: Which service generates the most noise, and what would it be worth to cut triage time there?
then.next: Baseline MTTR (M).

branches.if: "We have an SRE vendor or tooling"
branches.say: How does it go from detection to fix today? Where does a person still do the digging?

then.say: That is where Devin fits: investigation and the fix, alongside your existing tools.
then.next: Map integration points (D).

then.say: What about the code fix itself? Who writes and tests it?
then.next: Position the fix-to-PR step (D).
